concepts.title: From Alchemy to Chemistry
concepts.definition: Modern chemistry evolved from alchemy and iatrochemistry during 1300-1600 CE, and alchemy itself first developed in ancient Egypt, tied to beliefs in life after death and practices like mummification. The chapter follows this long road from magical craft to scientific chemistry, with India's own alchemical traditions as part of the story.
concepts.key_idea: Chemistry's family tree runs through alchemy -- Egypt's tombs, India's laboratories and Europe's iatrochemistry all feed the line.
concepts.textbook_ref: keks108.txt opening (from alchemy to chemistry, 1300 1600 CE, iatrochemistry, ancient egypt, mummification)

solution_steps.explain: Alchemy sought transmutation and elixirs, developing laboratory techniques in Egypt and beyond.
Iatrochemistry applied chemical preparations to healing, shifting attention toward usable substances.
By 1300-1600 CE systematic experiment replaced mystery -- the road to modern chemistry.

concepts.title: Metallurgy in India: Iron, Steel and the Famous Wonders
concepts.definition: India's metallurgical record is famed: high-grade iron and the wootz steel that travelled to the world, the rust-resistant Delhi iron pillar standing for centuries, and zinc distillation at Zawar. These achievements rested on kilns, furnaces and empirically mastered techniques far ahead of their time.
concepts.key_idea: Furnace mastery made history -- wootz steel, the rustless pillar and distilled zinc are India's metallurgical calling cards.

solution_steps.explain: Wootz, a high-carbon crucible steel, was prized abroad for blades of exceptional quality.
The Delhi iron pillar's composition and forged structure built a protective film that has resisted rust for over a millennium and a half.
Zawar's upward distillation of zinc vapour solved a problem -- this metal's chemistry -- that Europe cracked only centuries later.

concepts.title: Chemical Practice in Daily and Ritual Life
concepts.definition: Chemical knowledge in India also lived in workshops and rituals: dyeing and pigments, soaps and sugars, glass and cosmetics, fermentation and perfumery. Texts recorded recipes and procedures, showing that chemistry was practised -- and documented -- long before it was named a science.
concepts.key_idea: Chemistry before chemistry -- dyes, glass, sugar and scents carried chemical know-how through workshops and texts.

solution_steps.explain: Dyeing, pigment-making, glass, sugar, soaps and perfumes all depend on controlled chemical transformations.
Texts and manuals recorded procedures, letting craft knowledge accumulate across generations.
What the crafts practised empirically, later chemistry would explain -- continuity of the same knowledge.

worked_examples.question_pattern: The Delhi iron pillar has stood for over 1500 years with little rust. Explain what this achievement demonstrates.

solution_template.explain: The pillar's wrought iron has formed a protective surface layer, resisting corrosion across fifteen centuries of weather.
Such purity and forging skill imply sophisticated control of smelting and working.
The pillar is standing evidence of ancient India's advanced metallurgical chemistry.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A dyer produces the same fast colour repeatedly without knowing molecular theory. Explain how his work is still chemistry.

solution_template.explain: Preparing the dye bath, adding mordants and fixing colour are controlled chemical reactions.
Recorded proportions and procedures give reproducible results without theoretical explanation.
Chemistry can be practised before it is theorised -- craft knowledge is chemistry in the workshop.
